Listen to this article Share Nigeria’s efforts to strengthen domestic internet traffic exchange are putting data centres, telecommunications operators and internet service providers at the centre of a broader push to improve connectivity, reduce dependence on external networks and support the country’s expanding digital economy. The issue will take centre stage at the 2026 Nigerian Peering and Interconnection Forum (ngPIF), scheduled for October 28–29 in Lagos, where regulators, network operators, data centre providers and technology companies are expected to examine how stronger local interconnection can improve internet performance and infrastructure efficiency. The discussions come as rising demand for cloud computing, digital payments, online content and emerging technologies increases pressure on the infrastructure that carries Nigeria’s internet traffic. At the heart of the debate is the extent to which internet traffic generated and consumed within Nigeria can be exchanged locally rather than routed through networks outside the country before returning to domestic users. Keeping more traffic local could reduce unnecessary routing, improve service delivery and strengthen network resilience. However, achieving these benefits requires closer coordination between telecommunications operators, internet service providers, data centres and content delivery companies. Adewale Adedokun, convenor of the Nigerian Network Operators Group (ngNOG), said Nigeria needed a more strategic approach to internet traffic exchange, content delivery and the infrastructure supporting digital services. “As Nigeria’s digital economy continues to expand, we must pay closer attention to the infrastructure and interconnection arrangements that underpin it. Keeping more traffic local, strengthening peering and improving access to resilient infrastructure are critical to building a faster, more efficient and sustainable Internet ecosystem,” Adedokun said. The forum is convened by ngNOG in collaboration with the Internet Exchange Point of Nigeria (IXPN) and the Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC). Read also: AI adoption is outpacing governance in Nigeria’s telecom sector, NCC survey shows Data centres face a growing strategic role For data centre operators, the push towards local traffic exchange reinforces the importance of infrastructure that allows digital services and content to be hosted and accessed within Nigeria. Data centres provide the facilities where businesses, cloud providers and other technology companies store and process information. Their proximity to users and their connections to multiple networks can influence how quickly and reliably digital services are delivered. However, having data centres within the country does not automatically guarantee that traffic will remain local. The outcome also depends on where content is hosted, the networks connected to the facilities and the commercial arrangements governing how traffic moves between them. Stronger interconnection between data centres, internet service providers and telecommunications operators could allow more domestic traffic to move directly between networks, reducing unnecessary routing through external infrastructure. For Nigerian businesses that rely on cloud applications, financial technology platforms, e-commerce and digital communication tools, improvements in routing and network resilience could support more reliable service delivery. The economic benefits, however, will depend on the volume of traffic that can be localised, the cost of interconnection and the willingness of infrastructure providers to invest in the required capacity. Telecom operators face coordination challenge Telecommunications operators and internet service providers are central to the localisation effort because they connect millions of users to online services and determine how traffic moves across their networks. Internet peering allows networks to exchange traffic directly, often reducing the need to purchase transit services from third-party networks. The commercial terms and technical arrangements vary, meaning that the benefits of peering depend on the networks involved and the traffic exchanged. For operators, wider domestic interconnection could improve network efficiency and reduce some avoidable routing costs. It could also help networks cope with increasing demand for video streaming, cloud services and other bandwidth-intensive applications. Yet, the process requires cooperation among companies that may have different investment priorities, network capacities and commercial interests. Adedokun said no single participant could address the challenges independently, stressing the need for operators, data centres, content providers, regulators, internet exchange points and technology companies to work together. The challenge for the industry will be translating that cooperation into practical arrangements that expand local traffic exchange and improve the reliability of digital services. Infrastructure investment remains critical Nigeria’s localisation ambitions also depend on the availability of resilient connectivity infrastructure, including fibre networks, internet exchange points, data centres and content delivery systems. Internet exchange points enable participating networks to exchange traffic directly rather than relying entirely on upstream transit providers. Their effectiveness depends on network participation, sufficient capacity and the availability of content and services that users want to access. Similarly, additional data centre capacity will deliver greater benefits when providers can connect efficiently with telecommunications networks, internet service providers and content platforms. The ngPIF programme is expected to examine internet peering and interconnection, local traffic exchange, data centres, connectivity infrastructure, content delivery, regional connectivity and regulation. It will also feature technical sessions, research presentations, panel discussions and fireside conversations focused on the infrastructure required to support Nigeria’s next phase of digital growth. The discussions are expected to address the changing national digital infrastructure landscape and initiatives aimed at expanding connectivity and strengthening critical infrastructure. However, the organisers have not announced specific investment commitments, quantified savings targets or a measurable goal for the proportion of internet traffic to be exchanged locally. For the industry, establishing such benchmarks would help determine whether discussions on localisation are translating into measurable improvements in network performance, infrastructure efficiency and domestic digital capacity. Even as more Nigerians come online and businesses adopt digital tools, the benefits of connectivity depend partly on how traffic is routed, where services are hosted and how effectively networks interconnect. Localisation is therefore not simply a question of keeping data within national borders. It also involves ensuring that domestic networks have the capacity, commercial incentives and technical arrangements to exchange traffic efficiently. For regulators, the challenge is to support an environment that encourages infrastructure investment and cooperation without creating unnecessary barriers to competition or connectivity. For operators and data centre providers, the opportunity lies in developing networks and facilities that can accommodate rising demand while improving the economics and reliability of service delivery. The October forum will bring these stakeholders together to discuss the challenges and potential solutions. Its broader significance will depend on whether the conversations produce concrete commitments to expand interconnection, strengthen infrastructure and increase the amount of traffic exchanged locally. As Nigeria’s digital economy grows, the ability to connect networks and deliver content efficiently within the country is becoming an increasingly important part of the infrastructure supporting that expansion. Royal Ibeh Royal Ibeh is a senior journalist with years of experience reporting on Nigeria’s technology and health sectors. She currently covers the Technology and Health beats for BusinessDay newspaper, where she writes in-depth stories on digital innovation, telecom infrastructure, healthcare systems, and public health policies.
